summary: Describes current best security practice for OAuth 2.0. It updates and extends the threat model and advice in RFC 6749, RFC 6750 and RFC 6819 to reflect experience gained since, covers new threats, and deprecates some modes of operation considered less secure.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9700 rewrites the security guidance for OAuth 2.0 in light of fifteen years of use. It lists what servers and clients must now do, such as matching redirect addresses exactly, using PKCE on every request, and never returning access tokens in the URL, and it explains the attacks behind each rule.

subtitle: What OAuth implementers should require today, and the attacks each requirement answers.

tldr.problem: OAuth was designed for a small number of servers with known addresses, and it is now used in much more dynamic setups with stricter security demands, so the original advice no longer covers what happens in practice.
tldr.mechanism: The document restates the core rules, updates the attacker model to name five kinds of attacker, and works through the attacks seen in the wild with the countermeasure for each.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9700 is BCP 240 and updates RFC 6749, RFC 6750 and RFC 6819. It deprecates the implicit grant and the resource owner password credentials grant, and requires PKCE support.

facts.label: PKCE methods that hide the verifier

today: RFC 9700 is a Best Current Practice document, BCP 240, and updates RFC 6749, RFC 6750 and RFC 6819; no RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. OAuth 2.1, still under development, is expected to incorporate its recommendations.

sections.title: Why the Security Advice Was Rewritten
sections.content:
Since its publication in RFC 6749 and RFC 6750, OAuth 2.0 has gained massive traction in the market and became the standard for API protection and the basis for federated login using OpenID Connect. While OAuth is used in a variety of scenarios and different kinds of deployments, four challenges can be observed.

OAuth implementations are being attacked through known implementation weaknesses and anti-patterns. Although most of these threats are discussed in the OAuth 2.0 Threat Model and Security Considerations, continued exploitation demonstrates a need for more specific recommendations, easier to implement mitigations, and more defense in depth.

OAuth is being used in environments with higher security requirements than considered initially, such as open banking, eHealth, eGovernment and electronic signatures, and those use cases call for stricter guidelines and additional protection. OAuth is also being used in much more dynamic setups than originally anticipated, creating new challenges that go beyond the original scope of the earlier documents. OAuth initially assumed static relationships between clients, authorization servers and resource servers: the URLs of the servers were known to the client at deployment time and built an anchor for the trust relationships among those parties, and the validation of whether the client was talking to a legitimate server was based on TLS server authentication. With the increasing adoption of OAuth, this simple model dissolved and was replaced in several scenarios by a dynamic establishment of the relationship, so that the same client could be used to access services of different providers or serve as a front end to a particular tenant in a multi-tenant environment. Extensions such as Dynamic Client Registration and Authorization Server Metadata were developed to support these dynamic scenarios.

Technology has changed as well. For example, the way browsers treat fragments when redirecting requests has changed, and with it the implicit grant's underlying security model.

The document introduces new requirements beyond those defined in existing specifications and deprecates some modes of operation that are deemed less secure or even insecure. It does not supplant the security advice given in the earlier documents, but complements them. Naturally, not all existing ecosystems and implementations are compatible with the new requirements, and following the best practices described in the document may break interoperability. Nonetheless, it is recommended that implementers upgrade their implementations and ecosystems as soon as feasible. OAuth 2.1, under development, will incorporate the security recommendations from this document.
sections.plainLanguage: OAuth grew up. The rules were written for a world where the app knew the URLs of the servers it talked to and where the main worry was the password in transit. Both assumptions broke, so the guidance is rewritten around the attacks that are actually happening.

sections.title: The Core Best Practices
sections.content:
When comparing client redirection URIs against pre-registered URIs, authorization servers must utilize exact string matching, except for port numbers in localhost redirection URIs of native apps. This measure contributes to the prevention of leakage of authorization codes and access tokens, and it can also help to detect mix-up attacks.

Clients and authorization servers must not expose URLs that forward the user's browser to arbitrary URIs obtained from a query parameter, that is, open redirectors, as they can enable exfiltration of authorization codes and access tokens. Clients must prevent Cross-Site Request Forgery. Clients that have ensured that the authorization server supports PKCE may rely on the CSRF protection provided by PKCE; in OpenID Connect flows the nonce parameter provides CSRF protection; otherwise, one-time use CSRF tokens carried in the state parameter that are securely bound to the user agent must be used.

When an OAuth client can interact with more than one authorization server, a defense against mix-up attacks is required. Clients should use the iss parameter as a countermeasure, or an alternative countermeasure based on an iss value in the authorization response, processing that value as described in RFC 9207. In the absence of these options, clients may instead use distinct redirection URIs to identify authorization endpoints and token endpoints. An authorization server that redirects a request potentially containing user credentials must avoid forwarding these user credentials accidentally.

For the authorization code grant, clients must prevent authorization code injection attacks and misuse of authorization codes. Public clients must use PKCE to this end. For confidential clients, the use of PKCE is recommended, as it provides strong protection against misuse and injection of authorization codes, and as a side effect it prevents CSRF even in the presence of strong attackers. Confidential OpenID Connect clients may, with additional precautions, use the nonce parameter and the respective claim in the ID Token instead. In any case, the PKCE challenge or OpenID Connect nonce must be transaction-specific and securely bound to the client and the user agent in which the transaction was started. When using PKCE, clients should use code challenge methods that do not expose the verifier in the authorization request; currently S256 is the only such method. Authorization servers must support PKCE, must enforce the correct usage of code_verifier at the token endpoint when a valid code_challenge was sent, and must mitigate PKCE downgrade attacks by accepting a token request containing a code_verifier only if a code_challenge was present in the authorization request. Authorization servers must provide a way to detect their support for PKCE, and it is recommended that they publish the element code_challenge_methods_supported in their Authorization Server Metadata.

The implicit grant and other response types that cause the authorization server to issue access tokens in the authorization response are vulnerable to access token leakage and replay, and no standardized method exists for sender-constraining them. Clients should therefore not use them unless access token injection is prevented and the leakage vectors are mitigated, and should instead use the response type code or another response type that issues access tokens in the token response, such as code id_token. This allows the authorization server to detect replay attempts and generally reduces the attack surface, since access tokens are not exposed in URLs, and it allows the server to sender-constrain the issued tokens.

The resource owner password credentials grant must not be used, because it insecurely exposes the credentials of the resource owner to the client. Even if the client is benign, usage of this grant results in an increased attack surface, since credentials can leak in more places than just the authorization server, and in training users to enter their credentials in places other than the authorization server. It is also not designed to work with two-factor authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the rules every implementation is expected to follow now. Match the redirect address character for character, never build a link that forwards the browser anywhere, use PKCE on every request, stop returning access tokens in the URL, and stop asking the user for their password.

sections.title: Tokens: Replay, Privilege and Client Authentication
sections.content:
A sender-constrained access token scopes the applicability of an access token to a certain sender, and this sender is obliged to demonstrate knowledge of a certain secret as a prerequisite for the acceptance of that token at the recipient. Authorization and resource servers should use mechanisms for sender-constraining access tokens, such as mutual TLS or OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession, to prevent misuse of stolen and leaked access tokens. Refresh tokens for public clients must be sender-constrained or use refresh token rotation.

The privileges associated with an access token should be restricted to the minimum required for the particular application or use case, which prevents clients from exceeding the privileges authorized by the resource owner, prevents users from exceeding their privileges authorized by the respective security policy, and helps reduce the impact of access token leakage. In particular, access tokens should be audience-restricted to a specific resource server, or to a small set of resource servers. To put this into effect, the authorization server associates the access token with certain resource servers, and every resource server is obliged to verify, for every request, whether the access token sent with that request was meant to be used for that particular resource server; if it was not, the resource server must refuse to serve the request. The aud claim may be used to audience-restrict access tokens. Access tokens should also be restricted to certain resources and actions on resource servers or resources.

Authorization servers should enforce client authentication where it is feasible in the deployment, and it is recommended to use asymmetric cryptography for it, such as mutual TLS or signed JWTs in the form of the Private Key JWT client authentication method. Asymmetric methods mean authorization servers do not need to store sensitive symmetric keys, making them more robust against leakage of keys.

The use of OAuth Authorization Server Metadata helps to improve the security of OAuth deployments: it ensures that security features and new OAuth features can be enabled automatically by compliant software libraries, it reduces the chances for misconfigurations such as misconfigured endpoint URLs or security features, and it can help to facilitate rotation of cryptographic keys. Authorization responses must not be transmitted over unencrypted network connections, so authorization servers must not allow redirection URIs that use the http scheme, except for native clients that use loopback interface redirection. If the authorization response is sent with in-browser communication techniques such as postMessage instead of HTTP redirects, both the initiator and receiver of the in-browser message must be strictly verified.
sections.plainLanguage: A token that has been stolen is only dangerous because anyone can present it. Binding a token to the client that asked for it, and to the one server that should accept it, makes a stolen token much less useful. The privileges on the token should also be as small as the application can manage with.

sections.title: The Updated Attacker Model
sections.content:
The threat model in RFC 6819 describes the threats against which OAuth deployments must be protected, and while doing so it makes certain assumptions about attackers and their capabilities. This attacker model is made explicit here and updated and expanded to account for the potentially dynamic relationships involving multiple parties, to include new types of attackers, and to define the model more clearly. The goal is to ensure that the authorization of a resource owner with a user agent at an authorization server, and the subsequent usage of the access token at a resource server, is protected, as well as practically possible, at least against the following attackers.

Web attackers can set up and operate an arbitrary number of network endpoints besides the honest ones, including browsers and servers. They may set up websites visited by the resource owner, operate their own user agents, and participate in the protocol, including operating OAuth clients registered at the authorization server and their own authorization and resource servers. It must also be assumed that they can lure the user to navigate their browser to arbitrary attacker-chosen URIs at any time, for example by injecting malicious advertisements or sending legitimate-looking emails. They cannot, however, read or manipulate messages that are not targeted towards them.

Network attackers additionally have full control over the network over which protocol participants communicate. They can eavesdrop on, manipulate and spoof messages, except when these are properly protected by cryptographic methods such as TLS, and they can also block arbitrary messages. An example of a web attacker would be a customer of an internet service provider, while network attackers could be the internet service provider itself, an attacker in a public Wi-Fi network using ARP spoofing, or a state-sponsored attacker with access to internet exchange points.

Three further types of attacker are named. Attackers that can read, but not modify, the contents of the authorization response, which covers open redirector attacks and mix-up attacks, insufficient checking of redirect URIs, problems on mobile operating systems where different apps can register themselves on the same URI, and URLs stored or logged by browsers, proxy servers and operating systems. Attackers that can read, but not modify, the contents of the authorization request, in the same manner. And attackers that can acquire an access token issued by an authorization server, for example because a resource server was compromised, or because an access token was sent to an attacker-controlled resource server due to a misconfiguration, or by social engineering a resource owner into using an attacker-controlled resource server.

These three typically occur together with either a web attacker or a network attacker, and attackers can collaborate to reach a common goal. Implementers must take into account all possible types of attackers in the environment of their OAuth implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names five kinds of attacker, from a website owner who can lure you anywhere, to someone on the network path, to someone who can merely read the reply or the request, to someone who gets hold of a token. The point of naming them is that each one implies a different defence.

sections.title: Redirect URI Validation and Credential Leakage
sections.content:
Some authorization servers allow clients to register redirection URI patterns instead of complete redirection URIs, matching the redirection URI parameter value at the authorization endpoint against the registered patterns at runtime. This approach allows clients to encode transaction state into additional redirect URI parameters or to register a single pattern for multiple redirection URIs. It turned out to be more complex to implement and more error-prone to manage than exact redirection URI matching, and several successful attacks exploiting flaws in the pattern-matching implementation or concrete configurations have been observed in the wild.

Insufficient validation of the redirection URI effectively breaks client identification or authentication, depending on grant and client type, and allows the attacker to obtain an authorization code or access token, either by directly sending the user agent to a URI under the attacker's control, or by exposing the OAuth credentials to an attacker by utilizing an open redirector at the client in conjunction with the way user agents handle URL fragments.

For example, assume the redirection URL pattern https://*.somesite.example/* is registered for a client. The intention is to allow any subdomain of somesite.example to be a valid redirection URI. However, a naive implementation might interpret the wildcard as any character rather than any character valid for a domain name, and so permit https://attacker.example/.somesite.example as a redirection URI, although attacker.example is a different domain potentially controlled by a malicious party. The attack then starts by tricking the user into opening a tampered URL that launches a page under the attacker's control, which initiates an authorization request with the client ID of a legitimate client and the tampered redirection URI. If the user does not see the redirection URI or does not recognize the attack, the code is issued and immediately sent to the attacker's domain. If the attacker impersonates a public client, the attacker can exchange the code for tokens at the token endpoint.

Redirection URI validation vulnerabilities can also exist if the server handles wildcards properly. If the client registers the pattern and the server interprets it as allowing any host residing in the domain, an attacker who manages to establish a host or subdomain in that domain can impersonate the legitimate client, for example through a subdomain takeover where an outdated CNAME record points to an external DNS name that no longer exists and can be taken over by an attacker.

Credentials can also leak through the Referer header and through browser history. A Referer header carries the URL of the page the browser came from, so if the authorization response is placed in the URL of a page on the client, that page can then leak the code or token to another site it links to. The authorization code or access token can also end up in the browser's history, in proxy logs and in operating system logs, and is then readable by anyone with access to those.
sections.plainLanguage: The place the browser is sent back to is the weak point. If the server accepts a pattern such as any subdomain of a domain, an attacker can often find a way in that looks like a match but is not, and the code is posted straight to them. The other leak is simpler: the code sits in the address bar, so it ends up in the history, in proxy logs, and in the Referer header of the next page.

sections.title: Mix-Up and Authorization Code Injection
sections.content:
Mix-up attacks can occur in scenarios where an OAuth client interacts with two or more authorization servers and at least one authorization server is under the control of the attacker, for example because the attacker used dynamic registration to register the client at their own authorization server, or because an authorization server became compromised. The goal is to obtain an authorization code or an access token for an uncompromised authorization server, achieved by tricking the client into sending those credentials to the compromised authorization server instead of using them at the respective endpoint of the uncompromised server.

The described variant assumes the implicit or authorization code grant with multiple authorization servers of which one is honest and one is operated by the attacker, and that the client stores the authorization server chosen by the user in a session bound to the user's browser and uses the same redirection URI for each authorization server. The user selects to start the grant using the attacker's server, and the client stores that choice and redirects the browser there. The attacker's authorization endpoint immediately redirects the browser to the honest authorization endpoint, replacing the client ID with the client's ID at the honest server. The user authorizes the client at the honest server, which issues a code and sends it back to the client. Since the client still assumes the code was issued by the attacker's server, it tries to redeem the code at the attacker's token endpoint, and the attacker obtains it. The attacker can then exchange the code for an access token for public clients, or perform an authorization code injection attack.

For the defense, clients must store, for each authorization request, the issuer they sent the authorization request to, and bind this information to the user agent. Storing only the authorization server URL is not sufficient, because an attacker might declare an uncompromised authorization server's authorization endpoint URL as theirs while declaring a token endpoint under their own control. One defense requires that the authorization server send its issuer identifier in the authorization response, and the client must compare the received identifier with the stored one and abort on a mismatch. The issuer information can be transported via a separate response parameter, or through the iss claim in an ID Token. The other defense uses distinct redirect URIs for different authorization servers.

Authorization code injection is the other attack in this group. An attacker who has gained access to an authorization code can try to redeem it for an access token, and in the case of a code created for a public client, can simply send it to the token endpoint. For confidential clients, the attacker injects a stolen code into the attacker's own session with the client, so that the client's session becomes associated with the victim's resources or identity. The attacker starts a regular authorization process with the legitimate client from their own device, and in the response of the authorization server to that client, replaces the newly created code with the stolen one. The legitimate client then sends the code to the token endpoint with its own credentials, all checks succeed, and the attacker has associated their session with the victim's resources.

The countermeasure recommended is to bind every authorization code to a certain client instance on a certain device in the context of a certain transaction. PKCE does this: when the attacker attempts to inject a code, the check of the code_verifier fails, because the client uses its correct verifier while the code is associated with a code_challenge that does not match it. PKCE also protects authorization codes created for public clients, because an attacker cannot redeem a stolen code without the verifier. The OpenID Connect nonce parameter is the alternative for OpenID Connect clients: the client binds the nonce to the user agent session and sends it with the initial request, the provider puts the received nonce into the ID Token issued at the token endpoint, and if a code was injected the two nonce values will not match. This only works if the client properly checks the nonce in the ID Token obtained from the token endpoint and disregards all tokens until that check has succeeded.
sections.plainLanguage: The mix-up attack works when an app talks to two different login servers and cannot tell which one answered. The code injection attack works when a stolen code is slipped into the app's own conversation. Both are answered by tying the code to one particular app on one particular device: PKCE does that with a secret the app keeps, and the OpenID Connect nonce does it with a value the app checks in the returned token.

sections.title: Stolen Tokens and Refresh Token Protection
sections.content:
Access tokens can leak at the resource server. A counterfeit resource server can phish an access token if the client sends it to the wrong place, and a compromised resource server simply receives tokens that were meant for it. Audience restriction limits the impact of token leakage: the authorization server associates the access token with the particular resource server, and the resource server is supposed to verify the intended audience, refusing the request if the token fails the audience validation. To prevent phishing it is necessary to use the actual URL the client will send requests to, so that if the attacker tries to use the token at the legitimate resource server, which has a different URL, the mismatch is detected. Instead of the URL, the fingerprint of the resource server's X.509 certificate can be used as the audience value, which would also detect an attempt to spoof the legitimate resource server's URL with a valid certificate from a different authority. In deployments where the authorization server knows the URLs of all resource servers, it may simply refuse to issue access tokens for unknown resource server URLs.

Sender-constrained access tokens bind a token to the client that requested it, so that a stolen token cannot be used without proving possession of a key. This is the strongest defence against misuse of stolen and leaked access tokens.

Refresh tokens are a convenient and user-friendly way to obtain new access tokens, and they add to security because they allow the authorization server to issue access tokens with a short lifetime and reduced scope. They are also an attractive target, because they represent the full scope of access granted to a client and are not further constrained to a specific resource. If an attacker exfiltrates and replays a refresh token, the attacker can mint access tokens and use them to access resource servers on behalf of the resource owner.

Authorization servers must determine, based on a risk assessment, whether to issue refresh tokens to a certain client. If refresh tokens are issued, they must be bound to the scope and resource servers as consented by the resource owner, to prevent privilege escalation by the legitimate client and reduce the impact of refresh token leakage. For public clients, authorization servers must use one of two methods to detect refresh token replay by malicious actors. With sender-constrained refresh tokens, the authorization server cryptographically binds the refresh token to a certain client instance. With refresh token rotation, the authorization server issues a new refresh token with every access token refresh response and invalidates the previous one, while retaining information about the relationship: if a refresh token is compromised and used by both the attacker and the legitimate client, one of them will present an invalidated refresh token, which informs the authorization server of the breach. The server cannot determine which party submitted the invalid token, but it will revoke the active refresh token, stopping the attack at the cost of forcing the legitimate client to obtain a fresh authorization grant.
sections.plainLanguage: A token that has been copied to the wrong place is a problem, so tokens should be tied to one server and to one client. A refresh token is worse, because it can mint fresh access tokens, so public clients must either bind it cryptographically or rotate it: each use issues a new one and cancels the old, so the second use of the old one is what reveals the theft.

sections.title: Clickjacking, Redirects and In-Browser Flows
sections.content:
The authorization request is susceptible to clickjacking attacks, also called user interface redressing. In such an attack, an attacker embeds the authorization endpoint user interface in an innocuous context. A user believing to interact with that context, for example by clicking on buttons, inadvertently interacts with the authorization endpoint user interface instead; the opposite can be achieved as well, with a user believing to interact with the authorization endpoint typing a password into an attacker-provided input field overlaid over the original interface. Such attacks can be designed so that users can hardly notice them, for example using almost invisible iframes. An attacker can use this vector to obtain the user's authentication credentials, change the scope of access granted to the client, and potentially access the user's resources.

Authorization servers must prevent clickjacking attacks. Countermeasures described in RFC 6819 include the X-Frame-Options HTTP response header field and frame-busting JavaScript, and in addition authorization servers should use Content Security Policy level 2 or greater. To be effective, the policy must be used on the authorization endpoint and, if applicable, other endpoints used to authenticate the user and authorize the client, such as login pages and error pages. Because some user agents do not support Content Security Policy level 2, this technique should be combined with others unless such legacy user agents are explicitly unsupported by the authorization server.

Open redirection is covered by the rule that clients and authorization servers must not expose URLs that forward the user's browser to arbitrary URIs obtained from a query parameter. A 307 redirect also has to be handled carefully: an authorization server that redirects a request potentially containing user credentials must avoid forwarding those user credentials accidentally.

For in-browser communication flows, where the authorization response is sent with postMessage instead of an HTTP redirect, authorization servers must compare client receiver origins against pre-registered origins using exact string matching, and must send postMessages to trusted client receiver origins. Wildcard origins like * in postMessage must not be used, as attackers can use them to leak a victim's in-browser message to malicious origins. Clients must prevent injection of in-browser messages on the client receiver endpoint, using exact string matching to compare the initiator origin of an in-browser message with the authorization server origin. Since in-browser communication flows only apply a different communication technique, all the measures protecting the authorization response must be applied equally.
sections.plainLanguage: Three last ways in. A page can be laid invisibly over the login box so the user clicks the wrong thing. A link can be built that forwards the browser to wherever the attacker wants. And an app that receives the answer in the browser rather than by a redirect must check exactly who sent it, and must never accept a wildcard destination.

viz.caption: THE CORE BEST PRACTICES IN ONE PLACE

items.title: Exact redirect URI matching
items.text: Compare character for character, except the port in a native app's localhost URI.

items.title: No open redirectors
items.text: Do not expose endpoints that forward the browser to an arbitrary URI taken from a query parameter.

items.title: CSRF protection
items.text: One-time use state tokens bound to the user agent, unless PKCE or the OpenID Connect nonce is used.

items.title: Mix-up defence
items.text: Identify the issuer in the response, or use a distinct redirect URI per authorization server.

items.title: PKCE everywhere
items.text: Required for public clients, recommended for confidential clients, and required to be supported by servers.

items.title: No implicit grant
items.text: Use the authorization code grant, so access tokens stay out of URLs.

items.title: No password grant
items.text: The resource owner password credentials grant must not be used.

items.title: Sender-constrained tokens
items.text: Bind tokens to the client so that a stolen token is of little use.

viz.caption: THE FIVE ATTACKERS IN THE UPDATED MODEL

items.title: A1 Web attacker
items.text: Runs websites, browsers and servers, and can lure the user to any URI, but cannot read messages not addressed to it.

items.title: A2 Network attacker
items.text: Controls the network: can eavesdrop, alter and block messages unless cryptography protects them.

items.title: A3 Can read the response
items.text: Sees the authorization response without being able to change it, for example through an open redirect or browser history.

items.title: A4 Can read the request
items.text: Sees the authorization request without being able to change it.

items.title: A5 Obtains an access token
items.text: Gets hold of an issued access token, for example from a compromised resource server.

viz.caption: TWO ATTACKS ON THE AUTHORIZATION CODE, AND WHAT STOPS EACH

cells: Tricks the client into sending the code to an attacker-controlled authorization server
Identify the issuer in the response, or use a distinct redirect URI per server
Puts a stolen code into the client's own session, so the client receives the victim's tokens
PKCE, or the OpenID Connect nonce checked in the ID Token

viz.caption: FOUR WAYS TO MAKE A STOLEN TOKEN USELESS

items.title: Sender-constrained access tokens
items.text: The client must prove knowledge of a secret before the token is accepted.

items.title: Audience-restricted access tokens
items.text: The token is tied to one resource server, which checks the audience on every request.

items.title: Least privilege
items.text: The token's privileges are limited to what the application needs.

items.title: Refresh token rotation
items.text: Every refresh issues a new refresh token and invalidates the old one, so a second use reveals the theft.
